Dermatology · published research

Diabetic dermopathy

In a 12-person split-body pilot, lesion diameter and skin blood-flow measures favored the treated side, although lesion diameter also improved with sham. A separate case combined laser treatment with exercise.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In a 12-person split-body pilot, lesion diameter and skin blood-flow measures favored the treated side, although lesion diameter also improved with sham. A separate case combined laser treatment with exercise.

Summary of the Evidence

Two human publications address diabetic dermopathy: a 12-person placebo-controlled split-body pilot and one case report. The pilot compared active treatment with sham within participants but did not describe random allocation. The case combined light with exercise. No animal or standalone laboratory study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Twelve adults with type 2 diabetes and bilateral lesions received active laser on one side and sham on the other. Both sides also received skin care, including debridement, antibiotic cream, and betadine dressings. After four weeks, lesion diameter improved on both sides. Skin blood flow improved significantly on the active side but not the placebo side, and between-side comparisons favored treatment (Abdelhalim et al. 2020).

A case report described one person who received laser and specific exercises. The authors reported normalized skin color by day 21 and improvement in neuropathy findings. The case cannot separate light from exercise, other care, or natural change (Hazari et al. 2017).

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The pilot used 632-nm red visible light at 2.5 J/cm² and 0.02 W/cm², scaled to about 120 seconds per cm². Twelve sessions were given over four weeks. The case used 830-nm near-infrared light daily for 21 days, but some dose details are uncertain. These are different regimens, not a wavelength comparison.

Interpretation

The treated side had stronger blood-flow changes, while lesion diameter also improved with sham. Shared skin care and the small sample limit attribution. These findings support further study of local outcomes, not a settled treatment effect.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term lesion diameter and skin blood-flow changes
Publications and records2 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A 12-person split-body pilot compared treated and sham sides and found that blood-flow measures favored the treated side, while lesion diameter also improved on the sham side. Skincare was given to both sides, and the allocation method was not described as randomized. A larger masked trial with standard care balanced between sides and longer follow-up would support a stronger rating.
